title: Free-body diagrams and Newton's laws
objective: Choose a system, identify external interactions, and solve signed component equations for its acceleration or support forces.
why: Kinematics describes motion; dynamics connects changes in motion to interactions. Most force problems fail before the algebra starts: the diagram contains a force on another body, omits an interaction, or assumes a support force without checking its constraint. You will build an explicit force inventory, solve signed component equations, and test whether the answer is physically possible.

prerequisites.label: Motion and relative velocity in three dimensions
Introductory physics preparation
prerequisites.note: The prerequisite course is under construction. This lesson includes the needed force vocabulary; use the free mechanics resource for additional preparation.

sections.heading: Choose a body and an inertial frame
paragraphs: A system is the matter included inside your chosen boundary. It might be one cart, two carts together, or a cart plus its load. An external force is an interaction received by that system from something outside the boundary. An internal interaction connects two parts within the boundary. Write the system choice before calculating; the relevant mass and force inventory must describe the same system.

For a constant-mass particle or the center of mass of a body, Newton's second law in an inertial frame is $\sum\mathbf F_{\mathrm{ext}}=m\mathbf a$. An inertial frame is one in which a force-free body has constant velocity. In ordinary laboratory problems, a frame fixed to the building is often an adequate approximation; this neglects small effects from Earth's rotation and orbital motion.

A frame translating at constant velocity relative to an inertial frame is also inertial. An accelerating or rotating frame generally needs additional apparent-force terms if you use its measured acceleration. We will avoid mixing those descriptions: even an elevator problem below uses acceleration measured in the approximately inertial building frame.

Newton's first law is also a test of an inference: zero net force means constant velocity, including the special case of rest. It does not mean that every force is zero. Conversely, constant speed alone does not imply zero net force, because the velocity direction can change. Circular motion will make that distinction explicit.

sections.heading: Name interactions before drawing arrows
paragraphs: For each candidate force, name both agent and recipient: Earth on cart, floor on cart, rope on cart. A free-body diagram of the cart includes those received forces. It excludes cart on rope because that interaction is received by the rope. A point diagram represents translation; positions of application will matter later when studying rotation.

Draw the selected object alone, choose fixed axes, and draw one arrow for each external interaction. Label magnitudes or components, distinguishing known values from unknown forces to solve. A velocity arrow may help in a separate motion sketch, but velocity is not a force. An acceleration arrow may summarize your answer, but it is not an extra term in the force inventory.

The net force is the vector sum of the interaction arrows. It is not another physical interaction to add to those arrows. Likewise, ma belongs on the other side of the equation as mass times acceleration; drawing both the actual forces and an extra force called ma double-counts the dynamical effect.

Components are an alternative representation of one force, not extra forces. You may draw gravity as one vertical arrow or calculate its components in tilted axes. Do not then add the original gravity vector again to the component sum. A useful audit is to count distinct external agents before and after resolving components.

sections.heading: Keep mass, weight, and a scale reading distinct
paragraphs: Mass m is positive and measures inertia in these models. Its SI unit is the kilogram. One newton is one kg·m/s², so dividing a force in N by a mass in kg gives acceleration in m/s². The direction of acceleration follows the net force, not necessarily the current velocity.

Near a planetary surface, the gravitational force is $\mathbf W=m\mathbf g$. With +y upward and g a positive magnitude, $W_y=-mg$. Mass does not change merely because the object moves to a location with a different gravitational field. Its weight magnitude mg does change. Use the value of g specified by the model; examples here use 10 m/s² for transparent exact arithmetic.

A scale detects a contact force. Its reading may be converted into a displayed mass using an assumed gravitational field, but the underlying force is measured in newtons. In an accelerating elevator, the scale's force can differ from mg. Motion upward by itself does not imply a larger reading: an upward-moving elevator slowing down has downward acceleration.

In ideal free fall, a nearby freely falling scale supplies no support force, while gravity still accelerates the object. A zero scale reading therefore does not establish that gravity is absent. The distinction is between gravitational force and the contact force often called apparent weight.

sections.heading: Treat normal force and tension as constraints
paragraphs: A normal force is the contact-force component perpendicular to a surface. Its direction follows the local surface geometry, not a universal upward direction. For a straight horizontal floor, the normal force on a cart points upward. For an incline, it points perpendicular to the incline. Its magnitude is determined by the dynamics and the contact constraint.

If a cart remains on a straight horizontal floor, its vertical acceleration is zero. With an additional upward force Fy, the equation is $N+F_y-mg=0$, so $N=mg-F_y$. The familiar N=mg applies only when there are no other vertical force components and no vertical acceleration.

An ordinary unglued floor can push but cannot pull the cart downward, so N must be nonnegative. If an imposed zero-vertical-acceleration calculation gives N<0, the contact assumption has failed. For a cart initially touching the floor with zero vertical velocity and Fy>mg, the actual normal force is zero and the initial acceleration is upward. At Fy=mg, N=0 and the cart is at a zero-force contact threshold.

A taut flexible rope pulls along its local direction; it does not push. Tension is nonnegative. Equal tension throughout a rope requires additional idealizations, such as negligible rope mass and an ideal pulley. A negative calculated tension warns that a proposed taut-rope constraint may be impossible. The next lesson develops coupled bodies and friction; neither is silently included in this frictionless contact model.

sections.heading: Resolve signed equations, then test the answer
paragraphs: For fixed Cartesian axes, use $\sum F_x=ma_x$, $\sum F_y=ma_y$, and $\sum F_z=ma_z$. Keep the signs of force components through the calculation. A negative acceleration component describes the direction in which that velocity component changes; it does not by itself say the object is moving in that direction.

Choose coordinates that simplify a constraint. On a straight incline at angle theta above horizontal, choose the parallel axis uphill and the perpendicular axis away from the surface. Gravity has components $-mg\sin\theta$ parallel and $-mg\cos\theta$ perpendicular. Check the limiting case theta=0: gravity is entirely perpendicular, with no component along the level surface.

A cart constrained to that straight incline has zero perpendicular acceleration. With an applied parallel force F and no friction, $F-mg\sin\theta=ma_{\parallel}$ and $N-mg\cos\theta=0$. A nonzero perpendicular applied force would change the second equation; a curved path would require further care about acceleration perpendicular to the path.

Before accepting a numerical answer, substitute it into every component equation, confirm N≥0 or T≥0 where appropriate, and check units. Compare a simple limit: remove the applied force, let acceleration approach zero, or set the incline angle to zero. These independent checks often expose a sign or system-boundary error that the algebra alone cannot detect.

sections.heading: Identify third-law partners by reversing agent and recipient
paragraphs: For the interactions modeled here, if A exerts force $\mathbf F_{A\text{ on }B}$ on B, then B exerts $\mathbf F_{B\text{ on }A}=-\mathbf F_{A\text{ on }B}$ on A. The forces are simultaneous, equal in magnitude, and opposite in direction. Their recipients differ. Calling one action and the other reaction does not imply a time delay or a preferred cause.

Earth on cart and cart on Earth are partners. Floor on cart and cart on floor are another pair. Weight and normal force on the cart are not partners, even if their vectors happen to cancel. Both have the cart as recipient, while the third law pairs forces exchanged by the same two interacting bodies.

Because partners act on different bodies, they do not cancel in the force sum for either body alone. They do cancel as internal interactions when both bodies are included in a combined system. Equal interaction forces also do not imply equal accelerations: each body's acceleration depends on its mass and its complete external-force sum.

To audit a claimed pair, write agent-on-recipient labels, reverse them, and compare the vectors in the same coordinate axes. Looking only for two equal opposite arrows is insufficient. To audit a free-body diagram, check that every arrow has the selected body as recipient.

sections.heading: Combine bodies without inventing a shared acceleration
paragraphs: For two constant masses, adding their individual equations cancels their mutual force pair. The right side is $m_1\mathbf a_1+m_2\mathbf a_2$. Define the center-of-mass acceleration as $\mathbf a_{\mathrm{CM}}=(m_1\mathbf a_1+m_2\mathbf a_2)/(m_1+m_2)$. The combined equation is then $\sum\mathbf F_{\mathrm{ext}}=(m_1+m_2)\mathbf a_{\mathrm{CM}}$. A later momentum lesson develops the center of mass in detail.

This equation does not require both bodies to have the same acceleration. For example, two carts pushing apart can have opposite individual accelerations and a stationary center of mass. If a rigid connection or a taut inextensible rope imposes a particular relationship between their motions, state and use that constraint separately.

A whole-system diagram often removes an unknown internal force from the calculation. To recover that force, return to an individual-body diagram after finding the relevant acceleration. Never combine one body's external-force list with the total mass of several bodies unless the omitted interactions have been properly canceled by adding all of their equations.

In the investigation, keep the cart as the system and record the three agents in a table. Compare a supported cart, a zero-normal-force threshold, a separating cart, and a cart with no floor contact. The calculation predicts initial acceleration only; it does not simulate later collisions or a full trajectory. Save a prediction and explanation in your notes before revealing the result.

examples.title: Add a complete force inventory in three dimensions
examples.prompt: A 4 kg body receives exactly two external forces, (8,-6,4) N and (-2,10,-12) N. Any gravity is already included in this complete list. Find its acceleration in the inertial coordinate frame.

steps.reason: Add signed components of actual interactions. The word complete prevents adding an unlisted gravity force again.
Divide every force component by the same positive mass.
Substitution recovers the entire force vector; N/kg has acceleration units.

examples.conclusion: Acceleration is (1.5,1,-2) m/s². The initial velocity was not supplied and cannot be inferred from these forces alone.

examples.title: An upward-moving elevator can give a smaller scale reading
examples.prompt: A 6 kg instrument sits on a scale in an elevator moving upward but slowing with acceleration -2 m/s². Take +y upward and g=10 m/s². Find the scale force, then compare ideal free fall.

steps.reason: The instrument receives an upward scale force and downward weight. Acceleration is negative because the upward motion is slowing.
The scale supplies less than the weight, leaving the required downward resultant.
At the free-fall limit the contact force is zero, while the 60 N gravitational force remains.

examples.conclusion: The scale force is 48 N in the slowing elevator. Its value follows acceleration rather than the sign of velocity. A free-fall reading of zero does not mean zero gravity.

examples.title: Resolve one weight vector on a frictionless incline
examples.prompt: A 2 kg cart is constrained to a straight frictionless 30-degree incline. An actuator applies 14 N uphill, with no perpendicular component. Use g=10 m/s². Find the uphill acceleration and normal force.

steps.reason: These are components of the single weight interaction in the chosen tilted coordinates.
The parallel net force is 4 N uphill.
The straight incline constraint supplies zero perpendicular acceleration. The normal magnitude is positive and smaller than 20 N.
The component norm independently recovers the weight magnitude.

examples.conclusion: Acceleration is 2 m/s² uphill and the normal force is 10sqrt(3) N. The cart could still be moving downhill while slowing; acceleration alone does not specify velocity.

examples.title: Reject an impossible negative normal force
examples.prompt: A 2 kg cart initially touches a level frictionless floor with zero vertical velocity. An actuator applies (6,25) N, using +y upward and g=10 m/s². Determine the initial acceleration and actual floor force.

steps.reason: First test the proposed maintained-contact constraint rather than assuming its validity.
An ordinary floor cannot exert the required downward pull; contact cannot be maintained.
Use the actual external forces after rejecting the failed constraint.

steps.math: F_y=20\,\mathrm N\Rightarrow N=0,\ a_y=0;\qquad F_y=8\,\mathrm N\Rightarrow N=12,\ a_y=0
steps.reason: Compare the zero-force threshold and a genuinely supported state without imposing one formula beyond its domain.

examples.conclusion: The cart separates with acceleration (3,2.5) m/s² and zero normal force. The negative value from the first equation is evidence of a failed assumption, not a downward normal force.

examples.title: Separate force balance from a third-law pair
examples.prompt: A 3 kg box rests on a level table with g=10 m/s². List the two forces on the box, their third-law partners, and the net force on the box.

steps.math: \mathbf F_{\mathrm{Earth\ on\ box}}=(0,-30)\,\mathrm N,\quad\mathbf F_{\mathrm{table\ on\ box}}=(0,30)\,\mathrm N
steps.reason: Both displayed forces have the selected box as recipient. Rest is consistent with their zero resultant.

steps.math: \mathbf F_{\mathrm{box\ on\ Earth}}=(0,30)\,\mathrm N,\quad\mathbf F_{\mathrm{box\ on\ table}}=(0,-30)\,\mathrm N
steps.reason: Reverse agent and recipient for each interaction and reverse its vector in the shared axes.
Only the first two forces belong to the box's force sum. Their partners act elsewhere.

examples.conclusion: Weight and support balance on the box, but they are not a third-law pair. Their distinct partners act on Earth and on the table.

examples.title: Use a combined system without forcing equal accelerations
examples.prompt: Two carts of masses 2 kg and 3 kg form a system. Their net external horizontal force is 15 N. A mutual interaction has magnitude 8 N in each direction. Find the center-of-mass acceleration and assess whether the individual accelerations are determined.

steps.reason: Assign the equal opposite internal forces consistently to the separate diagrams.
Adding the equations cancels the internal pair; adding their unsigned magnitudes would be incorrect.
The weighted acceleration of the center of mass follows from the total external force.

examples.conclusion: The center-of-mass acceleration is 3 m/s². Individual accelerations require the distribution of external forces or an additional motion constraint; equal acceleration was not given.

guided.title: Build the inventory before solving for support
guided.setup: A 3 kg cart initially touches a horizontal frictionless floor with zero vertical velocity. An actuator applies (12,6) N in fixed horizontal and upward components. Use g=10 m/s² in an inertial frame.
before: Choose the cart alone. Its external agents are Earth, floor, and actuator.
Earth contributes (0,-30) N and the actuator contributes (12,6) N. The floor contributes (0,N) with N≥0.
Test maintained contact using zero vertical acceleration, then use the horizontal resultant to find acceleration.

question.prompt: Find the actual normal force and both acceleration components. Identify the third-law partner of the actuator's force on the cart.

options.label: Earth's downward force on the cart
options.feedback: That force has the same recipient but a different agent. Reverse agent and recipient of the given actuator-on-cart interaction.

options.label: The floor's normal force on the cart
options.feedback: A support force is another interaction on the cart; it is not the partner of the actuator's force.

options.label: The cart's force (-12,-6) N on the actuator
options.feedback: The partner reverses agent and recipient and has the opposite vector. It acts on the actuator, so it is excluded from the cart's diagram.

hints: Vertical balance requires N+6-30=0. Confirm that its solution is nonnegative.
N=24 N keeps vertical acceleration zero. Horizontal acceleration is 12/3=4 m/s².
Reverse actuator-on-cart to cart-on-actuator for the third-law partner; it acts on a different body.
explanation: The supported solution is feasible: N=24 N≥0. The force sum on the cart is (12,6+24-30)=(12,0) N, so acceleration is (4,0) m/s².
The partner of the applied force is (-12,-6) N exerted by the cart on the actuator. Including it in the cart's own force sum would erase a real interaction by mixing recipients.
question.answerSummary: Normal force 24 N; acceleration (4,0) m/s²; the partner is the cart's force (-12,-6) N on the actuator.

guided.after: Check all components by multiplying acceleration by mass: 3(4,0)=(12,0) N. Assuming N=mg would give an unbalanced upward 6 N and contradict the maintained-contact state.

interaction.prompt: Predict the support force, both acceleration components, and contact state before revealing a force inventory. Increase the upward applied force through the weight magnitude, then remove the floor and explain the difference.

summary: State the system and inertial frame; keep the force inventory and mass consistent with the boundary.
Include actual external interactions received by the chosen system. Net force and ma are not additional interactions.
Use signed component equations and distinguish acceleration from velocity.
Mass is measured in kg, weight is a gravitational force in N, and a scale detects a contact force.
Normal force follows the constraint and other applied forces; it need not equal mg. Reject negative values for ordinary unilateral contact.
Third-law partners exchange agent and recipient, act on different bodies, and have equal opposite vectors.
Internal force pairs cancel in a combined system. The resulting acceleration is that of its center of mass unless a shared-motion constraint is also established.
Check the answer by substitution, units, simple limits, and feasibility of every contact or rope constraint.
retrieval: A 4 kg cart initially touches a level frictionless floor. Gravity is 10 m/s² and an actuator applies (-8,10) N. Find the normal force and acceleration, then raise only the upward component to 44 N. Check after working: initially N=30 N and a=(-2,0) m/s². With the stronger upward force, maintained contact would require N=-4 N; actual N=0 and a=(-2,1) m/s², so contact is lost. The third-law partner of the second actuator force is (8,-44) N on the actuator.
